documents.title: Academic Integrity (Undergraduate Catalog)
documents.summary: The undergraduate catalog academic-integrity policy defines misconduct, with unauthorized AI use and uses of generative AI without explicit instructor permission counted as dishonesty. It lays out sanctions, reporting to the Provost, and a multi-step appeal process; AI appears only in the misconduct definitions.
documents.stance_why: The definitions list "artificial intelligence, etc. without instructor’s permission" and "generative AI tools ... without explicit permission from the instructor" as dishonesty, so AI is barred unless the instructor permits it, which is restrict.

units.why: The principles passage grounds the rules in "honesty, trust, fairness, respect, and responsibility", a fairness and integrity-culture reason, so P95 rather than skill-building P41.
units.anchor: foster a shared culture of honesty, trust, fairness, respect, and responsibility in all academic work
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded actor admin, coder B all. The sentence "We seek to foster a shared culture of honesty, trust, fairness, respect, and responsibility in all academic work" states a principle for the whole university community, so actor is all; both coders agree on P95, general, informs.

units.why: "Students are responsible for the honest completion and representation of their work" binds students to own what they submit, so P29 (own everything submitted).
units.anchor: Students are responsible for the honest completion and representation of their work

units.why: This bullet lists "artificial intelligence" among unauthorized materials "without instructor’s permission", making AI banned unless the instructor permits it. I chose P06 (default when permission is absent) over P36 because the distinctive content is the permission-based default; the misconduct label is coded in the next unit.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence, etc. without instructor’s permission
units.fit_note: Applies to all unauthorized materials (online sources, devices, social media, AI), not to AI alone.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded phase during-work, coder B general. The bullet lists "artificial intelligence, etc. without instructor's permission" among unauthorized materials a student uses, which concerns doing coursework, so during-work. Both coders agree on P06, must-not and restrict; A's fit_note (it covers all unauthorized materials, not AI alone) is kept.

units.why: The policy defines as dishonesty using "generative AI tools, such as chatbots, image generators, or code generators" for academic work "without explicit permission from the instructor", which classifies unauthorized generative AI as misconduct (P36) and sets an explicit-permission default.
units.anchor: without explicit permission from the instructor
units.fit_note: Also sets the default that AI needs explicit instructor permission (P06); one unit, one type.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded phase during-work, coder B general. The sentence bars generative AI used "to complete assignments, exams, or any other academic work without explicit permission from the instructor", which is about doing graded work, so during-work. Both coders agree on P36, student, must-not and restrict.

units.why: The sentence names "entering assignment or exam questions into AI tools to generate answers" as misuse, which matches P20 (do not feed assignment questions to AI).
units.anchor: entering assignment or exam questions into AI tools to generate answers

units.why: "Submitting AI-generated content as original work" is listed as misuse, i.e. AI may not produce the work a student submits as their own (P19).
units.anchor: submitting AI-generated content as original work

units.why: The definition of dishonesty includes "failing to disclose the use of AI in creating submissions when required", so failing to disclose is itself the violation (P28 over P24, because the sentence makes nondisclosure the offence). It forbids students from omitting required disclosure, hence must-not, and it takes a require position on disclosure.
units.anchor: failing to disclose the use of AI in creating submissions when required
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded modality must, coder B must-not (and unit_stance require vs neutral). The passage lists "failing to disclose the use of AI ... when required" as an act of academic dishonesty, i.e. something students must not do, so modality is must-not. The disclosure expectation it enforces is a require position, so unit_stance is require. Both coders agree on P28.

units.why: Sanctions "may be imposed by an instructor for academic misconduct" are listed (repeat the work, lower or failing grade); these are concrete penalties (P37), applied to AI misuse as part of misconduct.
units.anchor: A lower or failing grade on the assignment or test
units.frag_end: A failing grade in the course
units.policy: Instructors may impose, as sanctions for academic misconduct, an assignment to repeat the work, a reduced grade, a lower or failing grade on the assignment or test, a lower grade in the course, or a failing grade in the course.
units.fit_note: Penalties apply to all academic misconduct, not specifically to AI. Sanctions are for academic misconduct generally, not AI specifically.

units.why: For "egregious or repeated incidences" the instructor, dean or provost may impose an FX, suspension or expulsion, an escalation of penalties by offense (P37).
units.anchor: Permanent expulsion from the university
units.policy: In rare cases of egregious or repeated academic dishonesty or misconduct, the instructor, dean or provost may impose a non-deletable failing grade in the course (FX), suspension from the university, or permanent expulsion.
units.fit_note: General misconduct sanctions, not AI-specific.
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded the escalated sanctions as a separate unit; coder B folded them into one policy together with the instructor-level sanctions. They are two distinct rules with different actors (instructor, versus instructor, dean or provost in rare cases), so the separate unit is kept and its policy text is written to match the source list (FX, suspension, permanent expulsion).

units.why: "The student may not withdraw from the course to avoid the sanction" fixes a consequence in advance (P37), so a final-grade sanction cannot be escaped by withdrawing.
units.anchor: the student may not withdraw from the course to avoid the sanction
units.fit_note: General misconduct rule.

Talking with the student about the suspected misconduct before escalating is P57; P68 (educative response) fits less well because the discussion is about why a sanction is appropriate, not an alternative to one.

The passage tells instructors to discuss the importance of integrity and why a sanction is appropriate with the student before imposing it, which is a conversation before escalation (P57), not an educative substitute for a sanction (P68, which is the unintentional-error sentence). Both coders agree on instructor, when-misuse and should. A's fit_note (the discussion is about integrity generally, not AI rules) is kept. Coder A's fit_note for P68 was: Discussion is of integrity generally, not AI rules.

units.anchor: no later than ten days after the infraction is discovered

units.anchor: Instructors should file a notification of academic dishonesty regardless of the severity

units.anchor: has the right to a hearing before the academic dean

units.why: The dean’s conference is designed "to afford the student an opportunity to respond", a fairness step in integrity cases (P64).
units.anchor: afford the student an opportunity to respond

units.why: "A finding of misconduct must be based on a preponderance of the credible evidence" sets the standard of proof (P69).
units.anchor: A finding of misconduct must be based on a preponderance of the credible evidence

units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. "Evidence that bias by the instructor or dean substantially influenced the outcome" is one of the stated grounds for a due-process appeal, a real rule about students' recourse, kept as P64 with A's fit_note.

units.why: The Academic Integrity Appeals Board is a named body appointed by the provost that hears due-process appeals; naming who decides is P80.
units.anchor: The Academic Integrity Appeals Board is an ad hoc committee appointed by the provost
units.fit_note: Describes an appeals body for all integrity cases, not an AI-specific owner.

units.why: "The student shall have the right to be heard and to present relevant evidence" at the Board hearing is a right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: The student shall have the right to be heard and to present relevant evidence
units.frag_start: The student shall have the right
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. "The student shall have the right to be heard and to present relevant evidence" is a real student right in the appeals-board hearing, kept as P64.

documents.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Security and Privacy Policy, IT-5-136
documents.summary: An IT policy on generative AI security and privacy, covering workforce and students. It restricts non-public data in public tools, requires vendor agreements, defines key terms, names risks and sets responsibility; it is not about coursework rules.
documents.stance_why: The policy does not ban AI or make it available only by exception: it says "Exploring and benefiting from GenAI is in UMass Lowell's interest" and allows use under conditions (non-public data only under a binding vendor agreement, human review of output, user responsibility, disclosure). Coder A read the data limits ("may only be entered into") as restrict, but they limit what data can be entered, not whether AI may be used, so the document is permit with conditions. It is about data security, not coursework.

units.why: The policy says non-public information may be entered into GenAI "only when there is a legally binding agreement" reviewed through procurement, a data-protection rule with vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: non-public information may only be entered into, uploaded to, analyzed or otherwise processed
units.frag_end: sensitivity of the type of information.

units.why: "Non-public University information and data must not be entered into ... free, public GenAI solutions" is an explicit ban on feeding confidential data to public tools (P50).
units.anchor: entered into, uploaded to, analyzed or otherwise processed by free, public GenAI solutions
